projects.title: LangChain's knowledge factory: a librarian agent that keeps your agents' knowledge up to date
projects.what: An architecture where working agents (reports, content, GTM) rely on a company knowledge base that a dedicated agent maintains automatically. In short: an internal wiki nobody has to update by hand.
projects.how: The base holds 3 kinds of knowledge: skills (how the team delivers, e.g. writing a report in your style), domain knowledge (products, customers, competitors, what your KPIs mean) and data access guidance (which source to trust and how to pull from it). While working, agents have a tool to flag anything missing or wrong. At night, a curator agent (an agent running on a schedule) reads the flags, the traces (the log of what each agent did) and sources like Notion or Slack, then updates the knowledge. Only the curator writes: if every agent edited the base, it would fill up with contradictions. LangChain example: the finance agent spots a renamed database column and flags it; the finance lead asks for a new header on documents; the next night the curator updates the data-pulling skill and the report-writing skill, and every later report is right.
projects.who: Exactly an ops topic: company knowledge lives in people's heads; you give it to the agent once and it never forgets. Today's debate: @JohnKutay stores this knowledge in PostgreSQL rather than markdown files, and @scribeceo warns that documenting every workflow by hand is a huge job.
projects.try: It is a method, not a product. Minimal version suggested by @KevinMagnan: markdown files (Obsidian, Notion or GitHub), every new addition goes through a queue, and a cloud agent accepts or rejects the updates.

projects.title: Atlan Trident: a quality loop for your AI's context
projects.what: The product version of the knowledge factory, by Atlan (data catalog), announced at Context Conference.
projects.how: According to the link card, Trident shows how your AI uses your context (the information you give it), catches what breaks when you change models, and drafts the fix. Stated principles: knowledge managed as code (versions, dependencies), knowledge artefact types beyond markdown (ontology = the map of entities and their relationships, metrics, skills, tools), and hill climbing (improving step by step from traces).
projects.who: Companies with lots of data that want their agents to stay reliable from one model to the next. Mostly for large companies.
projects.try: Commercial product, price not disclosed. Site not reachable (t.co link blocked), limited details.

projects.title: Code mode in Factory: a daily Linear sweep drops from 245k to 23k tokens
projects.what: dex (Factory) plugged Procedural Tool Calling (PTC, code mode) into an agent that reviews Linear tickets every day. Result: 245k to 23k tokens and 7 min to 36 s.
projects.how: Instead of calling tools one by one and reading every full JSON response, the agent writes a small script that calls the tools, filters the data and returns only what matters. As dex explains, the model now only sees the Linear fields that matter for decision making instead of the giant gobs of JSON.
projects.who: Any ops automation that reads lots of data (CRM, tickets, emails). Fewer tokens is cheaper and faster, and the agent gets lost less.
projects.try: Factory is a paid product. The technique can be reproduced with any agent that can run code.

projects.title: Warp measures subagents: 40% more expensive, no quality gain
projects.what: Warp's founder compared two ways to organize his factory (a chain of agents that produces code): each stage delegating to its own subagents (sub-agents launched with their own context), or a simpler approach.
projects.how: On their setup, subagents cost 40% more with no meaningful quality gain. A 7-minute video shows the results.
projects.who: A common vibe-coder reflex is to multiply agents. Warp's data says: start simple, add subagents only if you measure a gain.
projects.try: Video in the tweet. Warp is a terminal with agents (free and paid plans).

projects.title: Chat with Work: work bots available in Europe
projects.what: A launch (planned for 'tomorrow' in the tweet) of work bots, pitched as the European alternative to Claude Duet (US only), ChatGPT's dots (not on Pro in Europe) and Gemini's Tasks (not in Europe).
projects.how: No technical details in the tweet. Available in the EU on every plan, or on your own servers.
projects.who: A French team that wants this kind of agent without waiting for the US giants, with the option to keep its data in-house.
